item.title: Calls for stronger national unity and deeper trust between communities - Roko Tui Bau
item.description: Fiji must move beyond historical divisions and mistrust and work towards building a nation where every citizen feels a genuine sense of belonging, dignity and equality. This was highlighted by Roko Tui Bau, Ratu Timoci Tavanavanua during discussions on the National Social Cohesion Framework saying no citizen should have to question whether they belong, whether they are welcome or whether they have
item.content:encoded:
Fiji must move beyond historical divisions and mistrust and work towards building a nation where every citizen feels a genuine sense of belonging, dignity and equality.

This was highlighted by Roko Tui Bau, Ratu Timoci Tavanavanua during discussions on the National Social Cohesion Framework saying no citizen should have to question whether they belong, whether they are welcome or whether they have a future in Fiji.

He says this requires communities to acknowledge the pain and experiences of the past, rebuild confidence and strengthen relationships through open dialogue and mutual respect.

Ratu Timoci says the gathering provides an important opportunity to reflect on the historical journey, cultural identity and contributions of the Indo-Fijian community to Fiji's development.

He says for more than 130 years, communities have lived alongside one another, sharing the same land, economy and contributing to the same nation, but this has not always translated into mutual understanding and trust.

Ratu Timoci says the Indo-Fijian community has made significant contributions to Fiji's economic development through agriculture, sugar production, small businesses, retail trade, entrepreneurship, education and professional services.

He says the resilience of Indo-Fijian families, despite periods of political instability and social tension, deserves recognition and respect.

He says Fiji has experienced four coups in the last 30 years, which have had lasting consequences on the country's progress, relationships between communities and people's sense of belonging.

He says these experiences have contributed to feelings of vulnerability and uncertainty among members of the Indo-Fijian community, with some feeling they have been treated as second-class citizens in the country they call home.

Ratu Timoci sa ys these experiences must be acknowledged with honesty and sensitivity, as recognising the pain of one community does not mean assigning collective blame to another.

He says reconciliation cannot be achieved by simply asking people to forget the past, but requires a willingness to listen, acknowledge harm, rebuild confidence and demonstrate that every person matters.

Tavanavanua says traditional and faith-based leaders have an important role to play in rebuilding trust and strengthening national unity.

H e says chiefs should send a clear message to all communities that Fiji is their home and that everyone has the right to live, raise their children and pursue their dreams in the country.

He stresses that national unity must be more than a statement or slogan and must be reflected through fair treatment, equal opportunities and meaningful participation by all citizens.

He says while Fiji's communities have learned to coexist, they must continue working towards deeper trust and genuine partnerships .

He says the dialogue process should continue beyond ceremonial gatherings through community discussions, joint activities, cultural exchanges and practical cooperation.

Ratu Timoci says the younger generation must also be taught to see one another through the possibilities of a shared future rather than the divisions of the past.

He says the ultimate success of the Talanoa session will not be measured by the words spoken, but by the relationships strengthened, assurances demonstrated and actions taken afterwards.

item.title: Dry weather leaves livestock struggling as grass dries up and land cracks in Ba
item.description: Prolonged dry weather in Fiji is making life difficult for livestock owners, with grass drying up and land cracking, leaving cattle and goats struggling due to a lack of grazing areas. Mohammad Raiyaz Khan of Talaiya, Ba, who owns Wananavu Kava Traders at the Ba Market, says the dry conditions have continued for a long time and are making farming increasingly difficult.
item.content:encoded:
Prolonged dry weather in Fiji is making life difficult for livestock owners, with grass drying up and land cracking, leaving cattle and goats struggling due to a lack of grazing areas.

Mohammad Raiyaz Khan of Talaiya, Ba, who owns Wananavu Kava Traders at the Ba Market, says the dry conditions have continued for a long time and are making farming increasingly difficult.

Khan says while his area is currently fortunate to have a reliable water supply, he is concerned about other communities in the Western Division that are already facing water shortages.

He is urging people to conserve water and avoid unnecessary use, particularly washing vehicles, to ensure there is enough for essential needs such as drinking.

Khan says people should prepare now rather than wait for the situation to worsen, particularly with the effects of El Niño expected to continue into next year.
